31: Lukáshka came slowly up to Maryánka.
30: “What swells!” said Nazárka, “Just like long-skirted choristers,” and he walked a few steps down the road imitating the soldiers. Again everyone broke into peals of laughter.
29: Maryánka began laughing and all the other girls chimed in.
28: “People are standing here, so you go round,” he muttered, half turning his head and tossing it contemptuously in the direction of the soldiers. The soldiers passed by in silence, keeping step regularly along the dusty road.
26: The tramp of regular footsteps at the other end of the street interrupted their laughter. Three soldiers in their cloaks, with their muskets on their shoulders, were marching in step to relieve guard by the ammunition wagon.
24: “No, my old one is sweeter,” shouted the Cossack, kissing the struggling old woman.
22: “Why don’t you hug Maryánka? You should do it to each in turn,” said Nazárka.
21: “I’ve heard say they’ll build a bridge across the Térek,” said one of the girls.
20: Maryánka, as was her wont, waited before she replied, and slowly raising her eyes looked at the Cossack. Lukáshka’s eyes were laughing as if something special, apart from what was said, was taking place between himself and the girl. “Yes, it’s all right for them as they have two huts,” replied an old woman on Maryánka’s behalf, “but at Fómushkin’s now they also have one of the chiefs quartered on them and they say one whole corner is packed full with his things, and the family have no room left. Was such a thing ever heard of as that they should turn a whole horde loose in the village?” she said. “And what the plague are they going to do here?”
19: Lukáshka all this time had stood silently looking at Maryánka. His gaze evidently confused the girl. “Well, Maryánka! I hear they’ve quartered one of the chiefs on you?” he said, drawing nearer.
17: “Just look, she doesn’t care. She’d howl, Nazárka, eh? Would she?” said Ergushóv.
14: “You’d have howled, I expect,” said Nazárka, laughing.
13: “There, they say girls have no strength, and you nearly killed me.” “Get away, you black pitch, what devil has brought you from the cordon?” said Ústenka, and turning away from him she again burst out laughing. “You were asleep and missed the abrek , didn’t you? Suppose he had done for you it would have been all the better.”
12: The Cossack stepped aside and nearly fell.
11: “What are you up to, you beast?” squealed the rosy, round-faced Ústenka, laughing and lifting her arm to hit him.
9: “Tell her,” shouted he. “That’s quite right what Nazárka says; a circular has been sent round. He can read, you know. Quite true!” And he began embracing the next girl.
7: “Now then, you black pitch!” squealed the girl, “I’ll tell your old woman.”
6: Ergushóv burst into a roar of laughter, and seizing the girl nearest to him, he embraced her. “I tell you true.”
4: “And I’ve also heard say that the girls will have to make the soldiers’ beds and offer them chikhir and honey,” said Nazárka, putting one foot forward and tilting his cap like Lukáshka.
3: “You don’t like it?” Ergushóv began again.
2: “Ah, ha! Have you met with trouble?” said Ergushóv. “I expect they have smoked you out with their tobacco?” asked another woman. “Smoke as much as you like in the yard, I say, but we won’t allow it inside the hut. Not if the Elder himself comes, I won’t allow it. Besides, they may rob you. He’s not quartered any of them on himself, no fear, that devil’s son of an Elder.”
1: “And I say so too,” put in the tipsy Ergushóv, laughing. “What a lot of visitors have come,” he added, pointing to a soldier who was passing by. “The soldiers’ vodka is good—I like it.” “They’ve sent three of the devils to us,” said one of the women. “Grandad went to the village Elders, but they say nothing can be done.”
0: “Well, God grant you get something good,” said the Cossack; “I’m glad of it, as I’ve just been saying.”
